lesson.menu_title: The Second Interview — What You Were Told in Round One
lesson.menu_desc: Reporting back what the panel and the headhunter said, and checking it with the CEO without sounding unsure -- 30 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 19 -- The Second Interview
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Fernando Meneghelli Bottura | Lesson 19 -- The Second Interview

listenings.text: When I call a candidate after a first round, I relay what the panel said, but I never read it to him verbatim. I tell him the chair said she would want to hear more about cash, or that one director had a reservation about his sector. Then I stop and I listen. The weak candidates get defensive, or they ask me who said it. The strong ones ask a different question. They ask what the panel might want to see in the second round, and whether they could send anything before it. That tells me they have taken the feedback on board, and it is usually the moment I decide to put in a good word with the chief executive.

I have hired four finance directors, and the second interview is the one I run myself. The first thing I ask is what the candidate heard in round one. Most of them gloss over it. The best one I ever hired opened his notebook and said, your chief people officer told me the role would include technology, and the headhunter said you might sell the print business. Is that still on the table? Two of those things were wrong. I corrected them in a minute, and we spent the rest of the hour on the real job. Secondhand information is not a problem. Taking it into the room without checking it is.

extra_audio.text: Rebecca asks what he took away from the first round. He says the chief people officer told him the role would include IT. She asks about the integration, and he says the headhunter told him she might want the new CFO to lead it. She confirms that the board will decide by June, and she says one director had a reservation. He checks one last thing: who the role would report to.
